text: Everything so far has mostly been about controlling what a model says. An agent — a model wired up with tool-calling access — can do things instead: send an email, modify a record, run a query, execute code. The moment a model's output can trigger a real action, the cost of it being wrong or successfully manipulated stops being 'it said something incorrect' and becomes 'it did something,' sometimes something you can't undo.

Nothing about the underlying reasoning gets safer just because tools are attached. Every indirect-prompt-injection and manipulation risk from earlier chapters still applies to an agent's decision-making — the only thing that's changed is that a successfully manipulated decision now calls a real function with real effects, instead of producing a sentence a human reads and judges for themselves.

Blast radius is the right frame for sizing that risk. Not 'could the agent be tricked' — against a motivated attacker, assume sometimes it will be — but 'if it is tricked, or simply wrong, what's the worst it can do with the access it currently holds.' An agent wired to one read-only lookup has a small blast radius: a bad decision returns a wrong answer. An agent wired to a broad credential and a destructive tool has an enormous one.

Least privilege applies per tool, not per agent. A lookup tool should use a narrow, read-only credential. A refund tool should use a separate credential limited to issuing refunds up to a defined amount, never a general finance credential that can also alter prices or close accounts. Scope it that way, and a prompt-injection attack that successfully misuses one tool still can't reach past that tool's own narrow permission.

Not every action should run fully autonomous, either. This is the same pattern Course 10 used for SOAR playbooks: propose the action, then have a human confirm before anything irreversible happens. Low-risk, reversible, read-only work can run on its own. Deleting data, moving money, sending an external message, or changing a production config belongs behind that approval gate, decided deliberately, tool by tool, up front.

And expose each tool as a narrow, validated function rather than a general-purpose execution capability — issue_refund with specific parameters, never 'run this shell command.' That structural limit on what the model can even request is a security control in its own right, and logging every call keeps a bad decision visible after the fact. Next lesson turns to the credentials those tools actually run on, and how to keep them out of the prompt entirely.
